An adapted tool also allows you to delegate certain tasks to your employees more easily, allowing you to focus on what is really important: the quality of your construction sites.

Automatic updates

Accessibility

Limited customization

Custom Solution

Full customization
: The software is designed to adapt to your business processes.
Data ownership
: You control your data and hosting.
Scalability
: You can add or modify features according to your needs.
The drawbacks of a custom solution are:
High initial cost
: Developing a custom software requires a larger investment.
Development time
: It takes time to design and deploy a custom solution.

The choice between a SaaS software and a custom solution depends on several factors:
Your specific needs

Your budget

content.text: I don’t trim hedges and I’ve never laid a single border in my life. My job is to build tools for craftsmen, and to do that, I spend a lot of time watching people work. Among landscapers, there’s one object I keep seeing almost every time: a Microsoft Excel file. A big one. Opened in the evening, at the kitchen table, after a day outside. A file that started simple but, over the seasons, has grown into a monster no one dares to touch anymore.
This article is for you if you recognize yourself in that description. Not to sell you a fantasy, but to show you, concretely, what can be done better.
Excel has been helpful to you—until the day it starts holding you back.

Let’s be honest: Excel is great at first. It’s free or almost free, everyone knows how to use it, and it does the job when you’re working alone on a few projects. The issue isn’t Excel. The issue is what we end up asking it to do.

You ask it to track your quotes, your schedule, your time logs, your supplier list, your maintenance contracts, and sometimes even your before/after photos stuck in a cell. But a spreadsheet wasn’t designed for that. So we improvise. We duplicate the ‘template’ tab, rename the file ‘quote_MartinV2_final_really.xlsx’, we end up with multiple versions of the same schedule, and one day a formula breaks without anyone knowing why, and a total goes wrong.
The real warning sign isn’t the complexity. It’s when the file lives on the office computer while you’re out on the job site, boots in the dirt, and you can’t check anything until tonight.
A landscaper’s quotes: where the money is made—or lost.
Let’s talk about quotes, because they’re often the most painful part.

A client calls you, you go over, take measurements, jot them down in a notebook. That evening, you open the old quote from a similar job, copy it, replace the lines, recalculate. You look up the current price of plants—the one from the last order at the nursery, not from another season. You adjust labor time based on your gut feeling. And you cross your fingers, hoping you didn’t leave an outdated line that doesn’t belong there.

Once sent, another problem arises: where is this quote at? Accepted? Rejected? Pending an answer for weeks? In Excel, there’s no reliable way to track that. You keep it in your head, and your head is already full.
A custom-built tool changes that—no magic involved. You start with a library of services that is
yours

: mowing, hedge trimming per meter, creating flower beds, planting—with your updated times and rates. You assemble a quote by putting together familiar blocks, right from your phone, even from the client’s garden if you want. And each quote has a clear status: sent, followed up, accepted. At a glance, you see what’s stalled and needs a call.
Job tracking: did this one actually pay off?
Here’s a simple question many landscapers can’t answer precisely: on the last big job, did you actually make a profit?

You estimated a certain number of days. But it rained, the soil delivery was delayed, you had to come back on a Saturday. Where are the actual hours? In the notebook, in team texts, in your memory. Nowhere centralized. So you never really compare what was planned with what actually happened. And without that comparison, you keep making quotes that are just a little too tight, season after season.

What a well-designed tool brings here isn’t surveillance. It’s memory. On every job, your crew clocks in their hours in two taps from the truck. The before/after photos are linked to the right client, not buried in your phone’s camera roll. The ordered materials are listed. At the end, you see if the job lived up to its promises—not to scold yourself, but to price the next one with real numbers, your numbers.

And those same details help beyond the job site: when the accountant asks for documents, when a client disputes an invoice, when you want to show a successful project to a potential client. Everything’s there, clean and retrievable.
The schedule: when the weather calls the shots for you.

A landscaper’s schedule is a living thing. It rains for days, and everything shifts. A new garden project falls behind, cutting into the weekly maintenance rounds. A client calls to move up their hedge trimming. On an Excel sheet, every change means manually dragging cells around, with the risk of forgetting to notify the right person.

And there’s this particular aspect of your trade that generic tools overlook: recurring maintenance. The lawn mowing and trimming contracts that come back at regular intervals, whether for private clients or co-ownerships. On Excel, you manually log them again and again, and sometimes a job slips through the cracks without anyone noticing—until the client does.

A tool made for you knows the difference between a one-off job and maintenance that should automatically reappear in your schedule. It knows that next week, it’s the turn of such-and-such a co-ownership. It shows you where your teams are, which jobs can be postponed if rain interferes, and what must never fall through the cracks. You keep the final say. The tool just handles what you can’t keep track of in your head.
'Custom-made,' concretely, what does that change?

You might think there are already off-the-shelf software solutions for construction. That’s true. Sometimes they fit perfectly, and in that case, I’ll tell you honestly rather than trying to sell you something else.
But 'custom-made' isn’t a luxury gadget. It means a tool that speaks
your

language. One that measures hedge length in linear meters and lawn area in square meters—not in abstract references. One that knows your services, your suppliers, how you break down a season. One that doesn’t force you to check fifteen irrelevant boxes designed for a plumber or a tiler. A tool that mirrors your trade, not your neighbor’s.

And most importantly: a tool that builds on what already works in your organization, without breaking everything. The goal isn’t to turn you into an IT specialist. It’s to free up your evenings and help you quote more accurately.
Your questions before getting started
Do I have to stop using Excel overnight?
No. We start with what you already have and progress step by step—beginning with what’s costing you the most time today. Nothing breaks all at once.
Will it take me a long time to learn?
The goal is the opposite: a simple tool, designed for your workflow—not for an IT specialist. If it requires a thick manual to use, we’ve gone wrong.
What if my business changes—a new hire, a new service, an additional sector?
It’s built to grow with you. A custom tool evolves; it’s not discarded at the first update.
Will my data stay secure with me?
Yes. That’s a priority we define upfront, even before writing the first line of code.
Can we review your organization together?

If this article resonated with you, here’s what I propose—no commitment. We’ll take a moment, over the phone or video call, and you’ll show me how you work today: your famous Excel file, how you create quotes, track jobs, and manage your schedule.

From there, I’ll give you a clear, written action plan: what’s truly stuck, what’s worth automating first, what can stay as-is, and where to start so you feel relief quickly. Not a technical tome—a document you understand and own, even if you later decide to handle it yourself or with someone else.
You know your craft better than anyone. My job is to make sure your tool stops holding you back and starts working for you.
Tell me about your organization, and I’ll get back to you quickly.

content.text: I’ve never pulled a wire or opened an electrical panel in my life. But I’ve spent evenings beside electricians who, once the last job was done, would sit down with a notebook and a phone full of construction photos trying to remember what they’d charged—and especially what they’d forgotten.

If you’re a self-employed electrician, or working with two or three guys, you know exactly what I’m talking about. The day goes like this: a repair in the morning, a renovation in the afternoon, a client calling at 7 PM because ‘it tripped again.’ And then there’s the paperwork, waiting for the evening. Or the weekend. Or never.
An electrician’s estimate is almost always a race against time.

A homeowner calls you to rewire their panel. You go take a look, measure everything in your head, jot down a few notes on a scrap of paper. Then comes the hard part: pricing it out—the materials, the hours, the code updates. But you’re doing it at night, exhausted, between other jobs.

Result? The estimate gets handed over two or three days late. Sometimes even longer. And in the meantime, the client has called two other electricians. The one who responds first, neatly, with a clear estimate? That’s often the one who lands the job—even if they’re not the cheapest.

Now, he opens his phone on-site. He creates the job in three clicks: client, address, what he did, the hours. The panel photo uploads automatically. At night, he doesn’t have to ‘re-enter’ anything—everything from the day is already there, and he just taps to turn each job into an invoice.

Julien didn’t become a manager. He just stopped leaving money lying around.

Not a bloated, overcomplicated system. A tool that does just three or four key things—the ones that matter to you:

Lost hours? They’re the small, unbilled jobs—where the money slips away.

content.text: In almost every B2B SME I step into, there’s one file. Just one. It’s called something like `suivi_clients_2024_V3_FINAL(really).xlsx`, it has fifteen tabs, and only one person truly knows how it works. When she’s on leave, the entire team holds its breath.

Excel is great. It’s often the right choice to start with: free, flexible, and everyone knows how to use it. The problem isn’t Excel—it’s when your business outgrows it without anyone noticing. Here are five signs that, when I hear them in meetings, mean the same thing: it’s time to switch to a real industry-specific software.
1. Multiple people need to edit the same file at the same time

This is the classic scenario. Two salespeople open the tracking file, each on their own, and by evening, you have to ‘merge’—meaning someone manually copies the other’s lines, hoping nothing gets missed. Or the file is on a shared drive, and you start seeing copies like `- Copy`, `- modified by Julie`, `- do not use`.

An Excel file was never designed to be a multi-user database. As soon as multiple hands start writing in it, you’re no longer working with data—you’re working with versions. A dedicated software solution, on the other hand, assumes that ten people are writing simultaneously, and that the data remains single and consistent.
2. You spend more time fixing than producing

A client billed twice. An order slipped through because it was on the next tab. A total that doesn’t add up, and no one knows why. If your team spends Friday afternoons ‘checking that everything’s okay,’ it’s not a discipline issue—it’s a structural problem.

Excel lets you write anything, including nonsense. A tailored tool puts safeguards where they matter: you can’t validate an order without a client, you can’t bill the same service twice, and a status can’t be both ‘paid’ and ‘pending’ at the same time. These invisible constraints eliminate errors at the source.
3. ‘That? It’s in Marc’s file’

When I ask where a piece of information is, and someone replies, ‘Oh, that’s Marc’s thing—it’s in his file,’ I know the company operates in silos. Sales tracking here, production there, invoicing in a third spreadsheet, and between them, copy-pasting and emails with attachments.

The cost of these silos is invisible but real: no one has the full picture, the same data gets entered three times, and when Marc leaves, part of the company’s memory leaves with him. A dedicated software solution brings all these pieces together in one place, where everyone sees what concerns them without having to ask.
4. There’s a formula no one dares touch
In every big Excel file, there’s
the

cell. A sprawling formula, written three years ago by someone who may no longer be there, that everything else depends on. No one truly understands it, so no one touches it—you just build around it, crossing your fingers.

It’s technical debt, exactly like in software, except it’s hidden in a spreadsheet, and the day it breaks, it breaks everything. When a company reaches this point, it’s the clearest sign that its tool has become more fragile than its business can afford.
5. You can’t answer a simple question in ten seconds

'How much have we billed this client since January?' 'Which orders are delayed?' 'Which salesperson signed what this quarter?' If the answer to these questions is ‘Give me an hour, I’ll make a pivot table,’ you don’t have a management tool—you have an archive.

A B2B industry-specific software solution is first and foremost about this: being able to ask a question about your business and getting the answer instantly. Not once a month when someone has time to compile it, but on demand, up-to-date, for everyone.
Crossing the threshold without breaking everything
The good news is that you don’t replace ten years of Excel in one weekend, and especially, you don’t have to. My approach is simple: start with
the file that hurts the most
, the one everything else depends on, and replace it with a tool that does exactly what it did—better, safer, and for multiple users. The rest follows, step by step, once trust is established.
I always give you
an honest budget estimate

if your Excel is still doing the job, I’ll tell you.
Switching to a specialized software should save you time and stress, not sell you a project you don’t need.

That’s a valid option, and I’ll let you know if that’s your case. Sometimes, a few automations are enough before considering real development.

What you’re really paying for in an agency

An agency is a team: a project manager, one or two developers, sometimes a designer, and a salesperson. This structure has real advantages — multiple people working on your project, continuity if someone leaves, and the ability to handle large volumes. But it comes at a cost, and you pay for that cost whether you need it or not.

Concretely, for a small business’s custom tool, a portion of the agency’s bill goes toward internal coordination meetings, layers of intermediaries, and a structural markup. It’s not theft: it’s the price of an organization. The key question is simple: does your project need this level of organization, or are you paying for an overbuilt machine for a need that could fit on three screens?

With a freelancer, you talk directly to the person who codes. No intermediaries, no telephone game between your needs and the result. You explain once to someone who will execute, not to a project manager who will ‘pass it up the chain.’ For business software where the devil is in the details, this is often what makes the difference between a functional tool and one that misses the mark entirely.
The rate is usually lower because there’s no structure to fund. And the responsiveness is better: one person, one point of contact, one to-do list.

But let’s be honest about the limits. A freelancer is one person: if they’re sick or overwhelmed, there’s no team to step in immediately. So you need to choose someone reliable, clearly define the scope, and ensure the code is yours and remains maintainable if you ever switch providers. A good freelancer will bring this up themselves; be wary of one who dodges the question.

what does my project actually need?
An
agency

is often the right choice if you’re launching a large platform with multiple features, if you need a guaranteed 24/7 support contract, or if the project will require multiple developers working in parallel for months.
A
freelancer

is often the right choice for a targeted business tool: automating a specific process, replacing an unmanageable Excel file, connecting two incompatible software programs, or digitizing a follow-up that costs you hours. In other words… the vast majority of the needs of a small business or SME.

If you’re still unsure, a good indicator: can you describe your need in one clear sentence? If yes, a freelancer will likely be faster and cheaper. If your need is vague and sprawling, a scoping phase — which I also offer — is better than rushing to the biggest option.

blog/logiciel-gestion-auto-ecole-plannin.metaDescription: Instructor scheduling, student tracking, hours, and payments: why custom software transforms the operations of a driving school. With a real-world example.

content.text: The first time I looked inside a driving school from the inside, what struck me wasn’t the driving—it was the wall. A large erasable schedule, instructors in columns, time slots in rows, and scribbles everywhere: a student shifted, an instructor is sick, a car is in the garage. Next to it, a binder per student and a notebook for hours. Everything fit in the manager’s head, and the day she took an afternoon off, no one knew who was supposed to drive with whom.

A driving school isn’t a complicated business. But it is a business with a lot of small, moving parts—dozens of students, several instructors, hours to track, payments spread out—and it’s exactly these small, moving parts that a custom software effortlessly absorbs.
The schedule: the real headache

A driving school’s schedule is in constant flux. A student cancels the day before, a time slot opens up, an instructor combines theory and driving lessons, a car needs to go in for inspection. On a wall schedule or a shared spreadsheet, every change triggers three more, and one oversight is enough for a student to show up at a closed door or two students to be assigned to the same car.

A tool designed for a driving school starts from this reality: at a glance, you see who is driving, with which instructor, in which car, and a freed-up time slot is automatically reproposed. The schedule stops being a source of anxiety and becomes a simple reflection of the day.
Tracking students: where is everyone at?

‘How many hours does he have left?’ In many driving schools, the answer is in a binder or in the memory of the instructor who follows him. As long as everything goes well, it’s fine. The problem arises when you need to decide who to present for the exam, follow up with a student who is falling behind, or justify a remaining balance to a parent who asks questions.

A specialized software keeps each student’s package, hours completed, progress, and documents in one place. Anyone in the driving school can answer in ten seconds without digging. And the student, for his part, feels supported—which matters more than you’d think for word-of-mouth referrals.
Hours and payments: where money gets lost

This is the most sensitive—and quietest—point. Hours completed but never invoiced. A package paid in three installments that gets lost in the shuffle. A student who ‘already paid,’ and no one remembers. Over a year, it’s not just a few euros: it’s a real share of the turnover that evaporates, without anyone having done anything wrong.

A custom tool links hours, packages, and payments: as soon as a lesson is completed, it’s deducted; as soon as a balance is due, it’s visible. You stop searching, and above all, you stop losing money.
A tool tailored for a driving school, not a generic calendar

There are calendars and off-the-shelf software. Some work perfectly well at first—and if one of them is enough for your driving school, I’ll tell you so honestly. But many managers end up twisting them to fit their needs: a field repurposed here, a spreadsheet alongside there, and you’re back to double the work.

Custom software does the opposite: it starts from your way of working—your packages, your rules, your organization—and fits it exactly. No thirty useless features, just yours, done right. And it’s built in stages, starting with what’s costing you the most time today.
FAQ
Is it worth it for a small driving school?
Yes, often even more so. Small businesses suffer the most from repetitive tasks because the manager does everything. Automating the schedule and tracking hours frees up precious time.
How long before the tool is usable?
We start with the most painful point—often the schedule or tracking hours—and a first version can be up and running in a few weeks, then we build on it.
Can we import our current data?
Yes. We start from your existing files and binders to initialize the tool: nothing is lost, everything is carried over.
What about the online theory test part?
We can either connect to it or leave it as is. The idea isn’t to replace everything, but to make the manual work around it disappear.

If you recognize yourself in the wall schedule full of scribbles, the simplest thing is to talk about it. I always start with an audit of your organization and a written action plan—you leave with something useful, even if we don’t work together afterward.

content.text: I don’t run a garage, I’ve never drafted a quote for roofing or managed three masonry projects in the same week. But after developing tools for tradespeople and small businesses, I’ve seen the same scene play out over and over. An Excel file opened on Sunday night, named something like `suivi_clients_v4_final_ok.xlsx`, that no one dares to modify for fear of breaking everything. And around it, two or three software programs that do the job ‘more or less,’ but none that truly fit how the business actually operates.

That’s usually when people talk to me about a ‘custom-built business application’—often unsure if that’s really what they need. This guide is here to clarify: what it is, when it’s worth it, what it actually changes, and how much time and money it requires.
What exactly is a custom-built business application?
It’s software built around
a specific trade and a specific way of working
— yours. Not a spreadsheet repurposed for another use, not a generic software where you’re forced to squeeze in using only one-fifth of the features.
In practice, it takes the form of a tool that tracks quotes, projects, and schedules for a
landscaper
, one that manages appointments, quotes, and vehicle tracking in a
garage
, or the module that connects interventions, quotes, and invoices for an
electrician
. The common thread isn’t the technology—it’s that
the tool fits the trade
, instead of forcing the trade to adapt to the tool.
Signs your business needs one
You don’t need an audit to spot them—they almost always show up in the same way:
You
re-enter the same information
multiple times—the client in one place, the quote in another, the invoice in a third.
Your Excel has become a mess that
only you know how to navigate
, and it crashes as soon as an employee touches a cell.
The information you need in the field
stays stuck in the office
— the schedule, the latest quote, a client’s history.
You spend your
evenings and Sundays
on administrative tasks instead of handling them during the day.

The real question is this: over your last busy month, how many hours did you spend copying information from one tool to another, or searching for a document you knew was ‘somewhere’? That’s the time a specialized app saves you.
What a custom-built application truly changes
The first change isn’t flashy—it’s subtle:
a single source of truth
. One client, one quote, one job exists in one place, up to date, accessible from your phone or your desk. No more three versions of the same file.

Then come the pleasant side effects. Quotes go out the same day because they’re generated in two clicks. Follow-ups aren’t forgotten because the tool reminds you. Copying errors vanish because there’s no copying left. And you present a more polished image to your clients—which, in many trades, matters just as much as the price.
Nothing magical about it: we take your real workflow and remove the friction, one piece at a time.
An example, to make it concrete

Take a plumber-heating technician with two employees. Before, every job relied on a notebook, a text message, and a corner of a spreadsheet: the appointment jotted down hastily, the quote typed up at night, the invoice sometimes forgotten for three weeks. Result: cash sitting idle and follow-ups you’re too embarrassed to make because you’re not sure who owes what.

With a tool built for him, the same day unfolds differently. He creates the job from his phone between projects, the quote turns into an invoice with one click once the work is validated, and his dashboard shows him in black and white which invoices are overdue every Monday morning. He hasn’t changed his trade—he’s just stopped losing it in scattered files.
Off-the-shelf or custom: the right reflex
Let’s be honest:
custom solutions aren’t always the right answer.
If an existing software already handles 90% of the work without twisting your arm, go for it—it’ll be cheaper and faster. Custom solutions make sense when your way of working
precisely
is what sets you apart, or when you’re already juggling multiple tools that don’t communicate with each other.
If you’re still torn between a simple brochure website, an off-the-shelf tool, and a dedicated app, I’ve broken down the decision in a
separate comparison
. The principle remains the same: we choose the lightest option that actually solves the problem.
How much does it cost, how long does it take
That’s the tricky question, so let’s answer it honestly. A
first useful tool
— not a bloated system, but the core piece that fixes the most painful issue — usually costs
between €5,000 and €15,000
, as a fixed price, and is delivered in
a few weeks
, not years.
The reason: we don’t build everything at once. We start with what hurts the most (often quotes or job-site tracking), put it in your hands
quickly
, and then add the rest later, once the tool is already saving you time. You fund the rest with the time the first version has given you back—not with a blank check upfront.
Once the tool is in place, maintenance costs
€100 to €300 per month
, depending on the tool. The price depends on the number of screens, users and connections to your software, and it’s set in the quote before we start. The details are on my
custom business software in Rennes
page.
How does a project actually unfold?
In practice, it comes down to four steps. We start by
looking at your current organization
— your files, your tools, your pain points. Then we
define
the scope of the first version: the bare minimum to make it useful right from day one. I develop, you
test in the field
quickly, and we
adjust
based on your real feedback — because a business tool is judged by how it works in practice, not just on a mockup.

I’m a freelance developer in Rennes, working with tradespeople and small businesses across France, and I remain your single point of contact from start to finish: no opaque subcontracting, no customer service on the other side of the world.
Frequently Asked Questions
Do I need to digitize everything at once?
No, definitely not. We start with the most painful point, and the rest follows if needed.
Will I be ‘locked in’ with the service provider?
The code and data are yours. The goal isn’t to make you dependent, but to make you self-sufficient.
Does it work on phones, on-site?
Yes. The field is often where the tool is most useful — so it’s designed for mobile from the start.

blog/ia-pour-pme-sur-mesure-agents-rag.metaTitle: Custom AI for SMEs: Your Data, No Fluff
blog/ia-pour-pme-sur-mesure-agents-rag.metaDescription: Answer queries from your documents (RAG), automate repetitive tasks (agents): what AI can truly do for an SME—practical insights.

content.text: For the past two years, everyone has been talking to me about AI. A craftsman who wants ‘something with ChatGPT,’ a small business manager afraid of missing the boat, a boss who tried a chatbot once and didn’t understand how it could help him. The word is everywhere, yet in most of the small businesses I encounter, AI still hasn’t made any real impact.

I’ll try to be honest because this is a topic where empty talk flows freely. AI isn’t magic—it won’t ‘run your business’ for you. But when properly connected to your data and your tasks, it can take a significant portion of repetitive work off your shoulders. That’s what it means, in concrete terms.
General AI doesn’t know your business

When you use ChatGPT as-is, you’re talking to a model that has read a large portion of the internet but knows nothing about you: not your quotes, your product sheets, your customer interactions, or your internal procedures. It answers well in general, but misses the mark on your specific case. That’s why many executives try it, get disappointed, and conclude, ‘It’s not for us.’
The real leverage for a small business isn’t general AI. It’s AI connected to your own data.
Answering from your documents (what’s called RAG)

Imagine an assistant who has read all your documents: your technical sheets, your sales terms, your past quotes, your meeting notes, your internal FAQ. When a customer or employee asks a question, it answers based on those documents, citing the source—not on generic information found online.

This is called RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). In short: the AI first finds the right information in your documents, then writes the answer based on that. The result isn’t a model making things up—it’s a model responding with your content.

For a small business, this makes a very practical difference: a new employee finding the answer on their own instead of bothering a veteran, a customer getting accurate information at 10 p.m., a pre-filled quote based on similar past quotes.
Doing tasks, not just answering (agents)

Answering a question is good. But the next step is doing the work. An agent is an AI you assign a multi-step task to, with permission to use your tools: reading an incoming email, extracting the info, filling out a form, drafting a response, and saving it as a draft for your approval.

The example I see working most often: sorting and preparing. Emails come in, the agent categorizes them, extracts attachments, fills in what needs to be filled in your tool, and presents everything ready for review. You keep the decision-making, and lose the chore.
The key word here is ‘draft.’ An AI well integrated into a small business shouldn’t act behind your back. It prepares, you validate. That’s what makes it usable without stress.
A concrete example
Take a 15-person SME that receives dozens of daily email requests: product questions, quote requests, customer service. Right now, someone manually sorts and distributes all of this.

With an assistant connected to their data: product questions receive a proposed answer, pulled from technical sheets, ready to send with one click. Quote requests are pre-filled based on similar past quotes. Customer service is prioritized by urgency. The person who used to sort doesn’t disappear—they shift from ‘copying and searching’ to ‘verifying and deciding,’ handling three times as many requests without losing their cool.
Custom-built or off-the-shelf tool?

Many small businesses don’t need custom development: an off-the-shelf tool with some built-in AI often suffices to start. I tell my clients this frankly. Custom solutions make sense when your data is sensitive (you don’t want to send it just anywhere), when your industry has rules standard tools can’t handle, or when you want the AI to integrate with your existing software—not the other way around.

In those cases, a solution built for you, hosted on your servers, connected to your tools, and following your rules, makes perfect sense. And it stays yours—not locked into a subscription you don’t control.
FAQ
Will my data go to an American tech giant?

Not necessarily. Depending on the sensitivity, you can choose models hosted in Europe, or even run certain parts on your own infrastructure. It’s a decision we make together, based on your constraints.
Do I need to be a large company for it to be worth it?
No. A small to medium-sized business with 10 to 50 employees, dealing with many repetitive questions or documents to sift through, is often the best fit: the time savings are immediate and obvious.
Will AI replace my employees?

Not with my approach. It handles the tedious tasks (copying, searching, sorting) and lets people focus on what they do better than a machine: deciding, reassuring, selling. AI prepares, humans validate.
How do I start without breaking the bank?

Start with one specific case—the one causing you the most trouble (sorting emails, handling customer service responses, searching through your documents). We’ll do it well, measure the results, and only expand if it proves its value.
Want to talk about it?

If you feel AI could help but don’t know where to begin, we can explore it together. I’ll start with an audit: which repetitive tasks cost you the most, what data you have, what’s realistic and what isn’t. I’ll provide a clear action plan and an honest budget. And if an existing tool already works, I’ll tell you.

blog/logiciel-rdv-auto-ecole-reservation.metaDescription: What if your students could book their driving lessons online without calling you? View available slots, receive reminders, and manage cancellations—your ultimate driving school guide.

content.text: A student who wants to book a driving lesson today often faces this: they call at 2 PM, but no one answers because the secretary is at the counter with a candidate. They call back at 5 PM, but it’s busy. They finally send a text to the instructor, who reads it between slots and forgets to note it down. Three days later, they show up for a lesson that doesn’t exist, or two students arrive for the same car.

I’m not an instructor, and I’ve never issued a driving license. But when I observe a driving school in operation, what stands out to me is the time spent on the phone playing receptionist. Scheduling an appointment, rescheduling it, calling back, shifting it again—these are dozens of small exchanges per week, and each one can get lost in the shuffle.
Booking always goes through you, all the time.

At most of the driving schools I encounter, there’s only one way to book a lesson: going through a human. The student doesn’t see the available slots, so they ask. You check the schedule, respond, and note it down. Multiply that by a hundred students, and you’ve got an enormous workload, all concentrated during opening hours—right when you already have someone in front of you.

The result isn’t just a waste of time. It’s also gaps in the schedule: free slots that no one books because no one sees them. It’s forgetfulness. And frustrated students who find it ‘complicated to book a lesson.’
What does online appointment booking look like?

A reservation tool designed for a driving school is simple for the student: they log in, see the truly available slots (the right instructor, the right car, the right duration), choose, and it’s booked. They receive a confirmation and a reminder the day before, and if they need to cancel, they do so themselves according to the rules you’ve set—for example, no cancellations less than 48 hours in advance.

From your side, you no longer have to manually input anything. The booked slot appears in the schedule and is deducted from the student’s package. You retain control: you open or close time blocks, block an instructor in training, and handle exceptions. But the usual flow—the one that used to consume your days—runs on its own.
A concrete example

Take a driving school with four instructors and 120 active students. Today, the secretary spends much of her morning on the phone scheduling lessons. Each instructor has their own notebook, and on Monday, everything is copied onto the wall schedule.

With online booking, the student opens the app from their phone in the evening, sees that Tuesday at 6 PM is free with their usual instructor, and books it. The secretary doesn’t discover the appointment the next day: she sees it filling up in real time. On Tuesday morning, a student cancels due to illness, the slot reopens automatically, and another waiting student receives a notification and takes it. No one called.
It’s not magic—it’s just the right tool absorbing the movements you used to handle manually.
'My students aren’t all comfortable with an app.'

This is the first objection, and it’s valid. Online booking doesn’t replace the phone—it frees it up. Autonomous students, often the younger ones, manage on their own and no longer call you. Those who prefer calling continue to call, but you can finally answer because the line isn’t clogged by those who could have booked themselves.
Booking, yes—but connected to the rest

Isolated appointment booking isn’t very useful. What matters is that it’s integrated with the rest of your management: the student’s package (a booked hour equals a deducted hour), tracking their progress, payments, and the instructors’ schedule—which I discuss in detail in
this article about a driving school’s schedule

. That’s where a tool designed for your profession—rather than a generic reservation calendar—makes the difference: it speaks your language (candidates, packages, driving hours, exams) and not that of a hair salon.
FAQ
Does it work for a small driving school?
Yes, and the benefits are often greatest there: when one person handles reception, scheduling, and check-ins, offloading reservations really changes the daily routine.
Can students book at any time?
No, you set the rules: open time blocks, minimum notice, number of hours per week, and managed cancellations. The tool enforces your rules—it doesn’t invent them.
Do I have to change everything at once?
No. You can start with online booking alone, let it run for a few weeks, and then connect it to student tracking and payments when you’re ready.
What if an off-the-shelf software already does this?

Then I’ll tell you. If an existing solution meets your needs within a reasonable budget, there’s no need to develop a custom solution. Custom development is justified only when your organization has rules that standard tools can’t handle.

If the phone ringing while you have a student at the counter speaks to you, we can explore this together. And if an existing tool is sufficient, I’ll tell you straight up.

blog/developpement-logiciel-b2b-sur-mesu.metaTitle: Custom B2B Business Software: What Does It Really Cost?
blog/developpement-logiciel-b2b-sur-mesu.metaDescription: Custom B2B business software costs €5,000 to €15,000 for most SME tools. The 5 price factors, the traps to avoid, and how to pay the right price.

content.text: Since I’ve been developing custom business tools for companies, the first question I almost always get is the same: "How much does a custom software solution cost?" The honest answer—the one no one likes to give—is: it depends. But "it depends" doesn’t help anyone. So here are the real factors that determine the price, concrete ranges, and the pitfalls that can inflate the bill.
Why there’s no fixed price

A custom B2B software solution, by definition, fits YOUR way of working: your processes, your rules, your terminology. Two companies in the same industry almost never end up with the same tool—and that’s exactly what makes it valuable. It’s also what makes every quote unique—just look at the variety of
custom business applications
, and you’ll see that none of them are alike.
What you’re buying isn’t lines of code. It’s time: understanding your business, designing, developing, testing, fixing, and deploying. The price is that time multiplied by a daily rate.
The 5 Factors That Determine the Price
1. Functional scope.
A tool that handles just one thing (a schedule, a case tracker) costs far less than a platform that connects quotes, invoicing, inventory, and customers. Every "and also…" adds days.
2. Users and roles.
A tool for just you is simple. As soon as there are multiple roles (admin, employee, client), permissions, and several people using it at once, complexity jumps up a notch.
3. Integrations.
Connecting to your accounting software, a payment tool, or an external API: each connection is a project in itself, especially if the other system is finicky.
4. Existing data.
Taking your current data—often a pile of Excel files—and cleaning it up to fit neatly into the new tool takes time, and it’s rarely factored into the first quote.
5. The level of polish.
An internal tool used by three people can tolerate a few rough edges. A tool your clients will see must be sleek, fast, and flawless on mobile. "Finished" comes at a cost.
Concrete Price Ranges
Here are my prices, on a fixed-price basis. Ballpark figures, not a quote:
A business tool for a small or mid-sized company
(scheduling, inventory, quotes, time tracking):
between €5,000 and €15,000
. A simple, targeted tool (one trade, one type of user, no heavy integration) stays at the low end of the range; several roles, integrations and a dashboard push it up.
A B2B platform
(multi-user, customer space, integrations, scalability): beyond that, and it’s split into phases.
Maintenance
, once the tool is live:
€100 to €300 per month
, depending on the tool.
What matters isn’t the absolute number—it’s the return. A tool that saves three people five hours a week pays for itself quickly.
These prices are net (VAT not applicable), and the exact amount is set in the quote before we start. To size your project, everything is explained on my
custom business software in Rennes
page.
The pitfalls that blow up the bill
The scope that grows along the way.
The ‘quick extra feature’ is the first item to exceed the budget. A good provider defines the scope and pushes the rest to Phase 2.
The initial ambiguity.
The less clear the need is from the start, the more back-and-forth—and cost—you’ll pay. A short scoping phase saves big.
Custom work when off-the-shelf would suffice.
Sometimes an existing tool covers 80% of the work. Coding those 80% from scratch is wasteful: you only customize what truly differentiates you.
How to pay the right price

Ship early. A first useful and delivered batch is better than a perfect project that never finishes. Release an initial version that solves the main problem, use it in real life, and then add what truly matters — not what you initially imagined.
FAQ
Isn’t a SaaS subscription cheaper?
Often, at first. But if the tool doesn’t fit your business, you’re paying a lifetime subscription for software you’ll have to work around. Customization is an investment that’s yours to keep.
How long does it take to get a first tool?
A targeted tool is often delivered in a few weeks to a few months, depending on the scope. Breaking the project into batches lets you have something useful quickly.
Do you need to define everything before starting?
No. Define the first batch precisely and keep the rest flexible. Trying to lock everything down upfront costs more, not less.
What about maintenance?
Software evolves: fixes, updates, enhancements. Count on €100 to €300 per month, depending on the tool. It’s the cost of keeping your tool reliable over time.
In summary

The cost of a custom B2B software depends mainly on the scope, users, integrations, and finish level. The real question isn’t ‘how much does it cost?’ but ‘how much does it save me?’ And the best approach? Start small, stay useful, then build from there.

content.text: "Do we buy an off-the-shelf software or have our own developed?" This is one of the first decisions when a tool is lacking. And it’s a real decision, not an obvious one: custom isn’t always the right answer, nor is off-the-shelf. Here’s how I help my clients decide without pushing custom development at all costs.
What each means
An
off-the-shelf SaaS

, is a pre-built software, rented on a subscription, shared by thousands of companies: a well-known CRM, an invoicing tool, a project management software. You adapt it a little, and you adapt a lot to it.
A
custom-built solution
, is a tool built for you, based on your rules, your terminology, your workflows. It does exactly what you need—no more, no less—and it’s yours.
Between the two, there are dozens of nuances (highly configurable market tools, custom modules integrated into a SaaS…). But the core decision remains the same.
When off-the-shelf wins (and we must admit it)
I’m honest with my clients: in many cases, an off-the-shelf tool is enough, and developing would be wasteful.
Your need is standard.
Invoicing, sending newsletters, managing a shared calendar—thousands of companies do the same, the tools exist, they’re reliable and affordable.
You’re just starting out.
Until your processes are stabilized, a flexible SaaS lets you experiment without committing to a development budget.
Time is of the essence.
A SaaS can be used tomorrow. Custom development takes weeks. If you’re in a hurry for a basic need, off-the-shelf wins.
Paying a subscription for these cases is the right move.
When customization is a must
Customization makes perfect sense when the shelf forces YOUR business to bend to ITS mold.
Your process is your value.
If your way of working sets you apart, a standard tool makes you ordinary. Customization protects it and speeds it up.
You’re already bypassing the tool.
Excel exports everywhere, repurposed fields, three incompatible software programs: signs that the shelf no longer fits.
Your data is sensitive.
You don’t want to entrust it to a third-party service hosted who knows where: a tool on your own infrastructure meets this requirement.
Subscription costs skyrocket.
With dozens of users, a per-person subscription eventually costs more than owning your own tool.
For the exact budget breakdown, I cover it in detail in
how much does a custom B2B software cost
— the real question always being, ‘how much does it save me?’
The Trap of the Two Extremes

Total customization, where you reinvent the wheel (a text editor, a calendar) is wasteful. Forced standardization, where you twist your business to fit a tool that wasn’t made for it, wears down your teams.

The right answer is often in the middle: a SaaS solution for everyday needs, and custom development only for what sets you apart — the unique business component no one else has. That’s where I focus my
custom business applications
that I develop.
My rule of thumb in one question
Before deciding, I ask just one question:
does this process make you better than your competitors?
If not (invoicing, counting, scheduling like everyone else) → shelf solution.
If yes (your method, your customer relationships, your production line) → custom development for that part.
The rest is just fine-tuning.
FAQ
Can we start with a shelf solution and switch to custom later?
Yes, and it’s often smart. We validate the need with a SaaS solution first, then develop only when we know exactly what’s missing. You pay for custom development only once the need is certain.
Is custom development only for big companies?
No. A small business with a unique process often stands to gain more than a large company with standard needs. It’s about specificity, not size.
Won’t a custom tool become outdated?
Like any software. The difference is that you decide when and how it evolves, instead of following an editor’s roadmap.
What if I make the wrong choice?
That’s why I start with a short, honest assessment. Sometimes I recommend a shelf solution and sell nothing — it’s better than developing something that won’t be useful.
In summary

Shelf solutions win for standard, urgent, or unstable needs. Custom development wins when the process is your value, when you’re already bypassing the tool, or when your data demands it. And the best approach is often hybrid: off-the-shelf for the mundane, custom for what sets you apart.

blog/logiciel-gestion-des-temps-feuilles.title: Time Tracking Software: Putting an End to Excel Timesheets
blog/logiciel-gestion-des-temps-feuilles.excerpt: Excel timesheets are costing you more than you realize. Discover the real, tangible benefits a dedicated time tracking software brings to a small business or SME.
blog/logiciel-gestion-des-temps-feuilles.metaTitle: Time Tracking Software: End the Excel Hours Hassle
blog/logiciel-gestion-des-temps-feuilles.metaDescription: Excel timesheets: errors, wasted time, forgotten entries. Learn how a SaaS-based time tracking solution truly transforms operations for SMEs—without unnecessary complexity.

content.text: How many hours did your teams spend on such and such client, site, or project last month? If the answer lies in a manually filled Excel file at the end of the month, from memory, you're losing money without even realizing it. Excel timesheets are everywhere in SMEs, and it’s almost always a false economy. Here’s why, and what a real time-tracking software changes.
The True Cost of Excel Timesheets
Using a spreadsheet to track hours seems free. In reality, it costs you:
Lost Time.
Each employee fills out their own table, someone consolidates the data, fixes broken formulas, and follows up with latecomers. Hours each month are wasted just counting hours.
Errors.
Data entered from memory at the end of the month, overwritten cells, wrong tabs. The numbers are approximate—and you invoice or pay based on that approximation.
Zero Real-Time Visibility.
You only discover a project’s budget overrun when it’s too late to react.
Nothing Actionable.
It’s impossible to quickly determine which client is profitable, which project is off track, or who is overloaded.
This isn’t an Excel problem—it’s a tool not designed for the job.
What a Time-Tracking Software Changes
A dedicated tool—often a SaaS—turns this chore into a habit. Specifically:
Entry Takes Seconds.
You start a timer or log your hours from your phone throughout the day, not from memory three weeks later.
Everything Is Automatically Categorized
by client, project, or task. The total is calculated automatically, without needing to fix formulas.
You See It in Real Time
where time is being spent: which projects consume too much, who is overwhelmed, what is billable and what isn’t.
Exports Are Ready
for invoicing and payroll in one click, with no manual copying.
The gain isn’t just comfort. It’s billable time you no longer lose, projects you can correct before they hurt your margins.
A Concrete Example

Take a ten-person agency that bills by time spent. With Excel, everyone vaguely fills out their table at the end of the month; the manager spends half a day consolidating everything and discovers that two projects have far exceeded the budget—too late.

With a time-tracking tool: everyone logs their hours in just a few seconds per day, the manager sees overruns developing along the way, follows up with the right client on time, and generates invoices with one click. Result: fewer ‘forgotten’ hours (and thus unbilled time), and projects managed instead of endured.
This is exactly the kind of need for which I design
custom business applications
: a tool tailored to how you track time, not a repurposed spreadsheet.
Off-the-Shelf SaaS or Custom Tool?

Let’s be honest: for a standard time-tracking need, an off-the-shelf SaaS does the job very well, and I often recommend it. Customization makes sense when your way of tracking is unique (specific billing rules, integration with other tools, or data you want to keep in-house), or when you want time tracking to integrate with a broader business tool you already own.
In that case, a custom time-tracking module tailored to your workflow, connected to your projects and clients, avoids yet another disconnected subscription.
FAQ
Will my employees accept time tracking?
If they already filled out an Excel sheet, yes—they’ll find it faster and less painful. The key is a simple tool: just a few seconds per day, from their phone, without unnecessary complexity.
Is it only for invoicing?
No. Even if you don’t bill by time, knowing where your team’s time goes reveals costly tasks, unprofitable projects, and workload imbalances. It’s a management tool.
How long does it take to set up?
An off-the-shelf SaaS can be up and running in a few days. A custom module takes longer but fits your rules exactly. We choose based on your situation.
What if I already have other tools?
A good time-tracking system integrates with what you already have (projects, clients, invoicing) instead of adding another isolated tool. This is often the real argument for customization.
In Summary

Excel timesheets cost time, errors, and visibility. A time-tracking software turns a monthly chore into a daily habit and gives you control over your business. For standard needs, a SaaS is enough; for unique tracking methods, a custom tool takes over.

blog/developpeur-nuxt-freelance-rennes.metaDescription: Migrating from Nuxt 2 to Nuxt 4, SEO, AI visibility, and custom business applications: what a freelance Nuxt developer near Rennes actually delivers for your projects.

content.text: When a company looks for a freelance Nuxt developer in Rennes, it’s almost never for a brand-new, smooth project. It’s a Nuxt 2 site that refuses to update, an application that’s been lagging since its last update, or an agency that built the tool three years ago and no longer answers the phone.

I work with Nuxt and Vue.js every day, having done so for several years: a daily-used back-office at Izidoor, showcase websites, business applications, and my own site. Here’s what I actually do when someone calls me about a Nuxt project.
Why use Nuxt for a website or business application?
Nuxt is Vue.js with everything needed to deploy a project cleanly: server-side rendered pages, routing, SEO, and translations.
For a business, this translates simply to:
fast pages
, loading before JavaScript even finishes executing;
good SEO
, because Google (and AI) receive real content—not a blank page to fill out;
a single codebase
for the homepage, blog, and connected space, instead of three poorly integrated tools.
And for small teams, Vue.js remains simpler to pick up and maintain than many alternatives. It’s a detail often overlooked when choosing a technology, only to be regretted two years later.
Migrating from Nuxt 2 to Nuxt 4 without breaking everything

This is the request I get most often. Nuxt 2 hasn’t been maintained since June 30, 2024, and Vue 2 since the end of 2023. In practice, no more security fixes, and dependencies failing one after another.
Migration isn’t an ‘update’ button. Here’s how I approach it:
A project audit
: which modules are no longer compatible, which pages are critical, and what can be simplified along the way.
A Step-by-Step Migration
: the Vuex store switches to Pinia, components gradually move to the Composition API, and each step is tested before the next.
A Smooth Rollout Without Surprises
: same URL, same SEO, and the ability to roll back if anything goes wrong.
The most costly thing is waiting: every month of delay adds another dependency to replace.
SEO and Visibility in AI: Where a Nuxt Project Makes the Difference
A well-configured Nuxt project is excellent for search engine optimization. Poorly configured, it can hide part of your content without anyone noticing.
Two examples from my own site, dibodev.fr, built with Nuxt 4:
Texts Invisible to AI Robots.

Some project descriptions were added via JavaScript after the page loaded. Google handled it well. But ChatGPT or Perplexity bots only read HTML: for them, these texts simply didn’t exist. Generating them during build fixed the issue—they now appear everywhere.
Overzealous Language Redirection.

A default setting in the translation module redirected all browsers set to English to the English version of the site. Google’s rendering bot was included: it saw my homepage in English. One line of configuration fixed the problem.
These are details you won’t spot by testing your site from your own browser. I check them systematically: what Google, Bing, and AI bots receive, page by page.
A Concrete Example: A Business Back-Office in Nuxt

At Izidoor, for nearly three years, I developed a Nuxt-based back-office used daily by sports and leisure clubs: activity scheduling, online payments via Stripe, statistics, and the reservation module their clients use to sign up.

This kind of tool isn’t particularly impressive from the outside. But a schedule that takes three seconds to load, multiplied by dozens of uses per day, is a team losing patience. A big part of the work is making the tool fast and intuitive: loading only the relevant data, keeping forms simple, and avoiding screens where you don’t know what to do next.
It’s the same approach I apply today to
custom business applications
that I develop for SMEs.
How I work on a Nuxt project
in Rennes or remotely
: I can come see you to define the project scope, then work remotely on a daily basis.
Fixed-price
for a well-defined project (a migration, a new application), with a clear quote: scope, price, and milestones set before we start.
Reusable code
: TypeScript, readable components, concise yet useful documentation. You’re never locked in with your service provider—including me.
Honesty
: If Nuxt isn’t the right fit for your needs, or if an existing tool already does the job, I’ll tell you.
My full background is on the
about
page, and my work on the
projects
Frequently Asked Questions
My Nuxt 2 site still works, why migrate?
Because it no longer receives any security updates as of June 2024, and its dependencies will continue to break one by one. The longer you wait, the more expensive the migration becomes.
How long does a migration from Nuxt 2 to Nuxt 4 take?

It mostly depends on the number of pages and modules. For a brochure site, it’s a matter of days. For a full-fledged business application, it’s more likely to take weeks. I always start with an audit to give you an accurate estimate.
Do you also work with Vue.js without Nuxt?
Yes. For a back-office or an application that doesn’t need SEO, a standalone Vue.js app can be sufficient, and I’ll suggest it if appropriate.
Can you take over a Nuxt project developed by someone else?
Yes, it’s actually quite common. I start by reviewing the code, identifying what’s solid and what needs fixing, before proposing a plan.
Let’s talk?

If you have a Nuxt project to launch, a Nuxt 2 site to migrate, or an application that could use a refresh, the easiest way is to discuss it. I’ll review your project and provide a written action plan with an honest budget estimate. And if an existing tool is sufficient, I’ll let you know.

blog/pass-commerce-artisanat-rennes-site.title: Pass Commerce et Artisanat in Rennes Métropole: Funding for Your Website
blog/pass-commerce-artisanat-rennes-site.excerpt: Up to €6,000 in aid: who qualifies in Rennes Métropole, what matters for a website, the minimum threshold to meet, and the scheduling mistake that can cost you the aid.
blog/pass-commerce-artisanat-rennes-site.metaTitle: Rennes Pass Commerce et Artisanat: Funding Your Website
blog/pass-commerce-artisanat-rennes-site.metaDescription: Running a shop or workshop near Rennes? The Pass Commerce et Artisanat can fund up to 30% of your project, including your website. Eligible municipalities, minimum requirements, and steps explained.

content.text: Saint-Erblon, where I live, is one of the 23 municipalities in Rennes Métropole where the Pass Commerce et Artisanat applies. In concrete terms, a baker, hairdresser, or electrician from one of these municipalities can receive 30% assistance on a modernization project, including a website.

On paper, it’s simple. Yet, there are three or four lines in the guidelines that change everything, and a scheduling error can be enough to lose the aid. I read it line by line with one question in mind: what does this mean for a merchant or artisan who wants a website? Here’s what I retain, without jargon. I verified this information in September 2026; rules may change, and the CCI (Chamber of Commerce) and CMA (Chamber of Trades) always have the final say.
The Pass Commerce et Artisanat of Rennes Métropole, explained
This is a subsidy from Rennes Métropole, in partnership with the Brittany Region, for small local businesses and artisans investing in: renovations, equipment, and digital solutions.
30% of approved investments;
up to €20,000 HT (excluding tax), meaning a maximum of €6,000 in aid;
for investments starting at €6,000 HT;
for a project completed within three years.
The regional program has been extended until 2028. The aid is paid out at the end, once invoices are verified: you must front the money. All details are in the
official guidelines of Rennes Métropole
Who qualifies? Not the center of Rennes

This is the point many overlook. In Rennes Métropole, the Pass does not cover the entire metropolitan area: it targets municipalities with fewer than 5,000 inhabitants and priority neighborhoods in Rennes, where businesses are most vulnerable.

The 23 eligible municipalities: Bécherel, Bourgbarré, Brécé, Chavagne, Chevaigné, Cintré, Clayes, Corps-Nuds, La Chapelle-Chaussée, La Chapelle-des-Fougeretz, La Chapelle-Thouarault, Langan, Le Verger, L'Hermitage, Miniac-sous-Bécherel, Montgermont, Nouvoitou, Parthenay-de-Bretagne, Pont-Péan, Romillé, Saint-Armel, Saint-Erblon, and Saint-Sulpice-la-Forêt.
Priority neighborhoods in Rennes: Villejean, Le Blosne, Cleunay, Clôteaux–Champs Manceaux, and Maurepas, within their official boundaries.

A store in the center of Rennes, Cesson-Sévigné, or Bruz does not qualify for this program. And in the 23 municipalities, a ‘window display’ business must also be located in the central area defined by the PLUi (Local Urban Plan), essentially the town center. A production artisan, like a cabinetmaker or a ceramist in their workshop, does not have this constraint.
For the rest, the business must:
be an independent retail or artisan business, registered with the RCS (Commercial and Companies Register) or RNE (National Enterprise Directory) (or an association registered with the RNA);
generate most of its revenue from individual customers in a local activity: bakery, café, restaurant, hairdressing, florist, cobbler, but also painter, electrician, or plumber;
have no more than 10 full-time equivalent employees (excluding the manager);
generate no more than €1 million in annual revenue (excluding tax).

Excluded, among others: liberal professions, medical and paramedical services, personal care services, real estate or travel agencies, shops in shopping malls or commercial zones, and fully online activities.
What the Pass covers for your website
On the digital side, the guidelines include:
the creation or redesign of a website;
an online sales module (ordering, in-store pickup);
a day of training to learn how to manage the new website;
digital or web visibility consulting for the portion that remains your responsibility;
computer equipment related to a digital project, such as a point-of-sale software.
What is not covered: hosting, maintenance, and subscriptions, creation of visuals, and advertising.

Two gray areas to confirm with the CCI or CMA before signing. Some consulting services related to a website are only covered if they accompany the purchase of digital equipment. And a custom tool, like an appointment scheduler or order tracker, is not explicitly mentioned: depending on its function, it may resemble a sales module or management software, but the chamber makes the final decision. If you’re unsure between the two, I explain the difference in
website or business tool: which to choose
The €6,000 threshold: a website alone rarely qualifies
This is the line people read too quickly. The Pass from Rennes Métropole starts at €6,000 HT in approved investments. However, a business website often costs less than that.
In practice, the website is part of a broader project: a refrigerated display case, a sign, accessibility renovations, or a point-of-sale software. Everything is combined in the same application.

Two additional conditions in Rennes Métropole. The application must include at least one investment related to CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility), such as energy-efficient equipment. And before submitting, you must complete an online CSR self-assessment, free of charge, provided by the Métropole.
A numbered example
Imagine a baker in the town center of Pont-Péan. They want to take online orders for Yule logs and crêpes, and their refrigerated display case is nearing the end of its life. Their project includes:
a website with online ordering and in-store pickup: €4,500 HT;
a new refrigerated display case: €8,000 HT;
switching the store lighting to LED: €1,500 HT, their CSR investment.

Total: €14,000 HT. The 30% aid amounts to €4,200. Hosting and website maintenance remain their responsibility. Alone, the €4,500 website would not meet the threshold: it’s the complete project that qualifies.
The mistake that costs you the aid: signing your quote too early
This is the classic trap. Quotes and invoices must be dated after sending your letter of intent on the Brittany Region’s platform. A quote dated before the letter means the expense won’t be covered.

The order is as follows: letter of intent, receipt of acknowledgment from Rennes Métropole, then signing the quotes. This acknowledgment does not guarantee the aid, but it authorizes you to proceed with expenses.

For the web portion, ask your provider for a quote dated after the letter, clearly separating website creation (eligible) from hosting and maintenance (not eligible). You’ll avoid back-and-forth with the chamber.
Steps to obtain the Pass Commerce et Artisanat
1. Verify your eligibility: municipality, activity, staff count, and revenue.

2. Call the chamber that oversees you: the CCI Ille-et-Vilaine (02 99 33 66 66) if you’re registered with the RCS or are an association, or the CMA Ille-et-Vilaine (02 23 500 500) if you’re registered with the trades directory.
3. Create your account on the
regional Pass Commerce et Artisanat platform
and send your letter of intent.
4. Wait for the acknowledgment of receipt from Rennes Métropole before signing anything.
5. Complete the online CSR self-assessment before submitting your application.
6. Gather your quotes and prepare your financing plan, including loans. The chamber will conduct an on-site visit.

7. Submit the complete application within 6 months of receiving the acknowledgment: a K-bis extract less than a year old, bank details, a statement from your accountant, financing plan, quotes, a minimis attestation (summary of public aid already received), and bank agreements.

8. Complete the project, then submit your invoices: Rennes Métropole will pay the aid after verification, and you’ll display a communication support from the Region and the Métropole on your storefront.
Outside of Rennes Métropole, each intercommunality has its own rules

The Pass Commerce et Artisanat exists in most Breton intercommunalities, but each adapts it. The regional framework offers 30% on up to €25,000 HT in expenses, meaning up to €7,500 in aid. Rennes Métropole chose €20,000 and €6,000, with its own conditions.

Some communities of communes go further on digital. For example, Bretagne Porte de Loire Communauté, in the southern part of the department, offers a 50% digital subsidy for a website project between €2,000 and €15,000. If your business is near Vitré, Fougères, Châteaugiron, or Liffré, check with your community of communes: amounts and conditions vary by territory.
What I do for your application, and what I don’t do
I’m an independent developer in Saint-Erblon. I create websites and custom tools for local merchants and artisans.
I don’t prepare your application for you—that’s the job of the CCI or CMA. My role is the digital part:
a clear quote, dated at the right time, separating eligible lines from hosting or maintenance;
a project description, detailing what the website does and for whom, which you can include in your application;
the website or tool itself, including a training session if you want one.
And if your project doesn’t meet the threshold or your business isn’t in an eligible municipality, I’ll tell you right away. It’s better to know before filling out paperwork.
Your questions about the Pass Commerce et Artisanat
My business is in the center of Rennes—do I qualify?

Not with the Pass from Rennes Métropole, unless your address is in one of the priority neighborhoods: Villejean, Le Blosne, Cleunay, Clôteaux–Champs Manceaux, or Maurepas. In case of doubt, the CCI or CMA will verify your address.
Can a website alone be funded?

Creating a website is part of eligible expenses. However, you must reach €6,000 HT in approved expenses and include a CSR investment: in practice, the website almost always fits into a larger project. The chamber will tell you if yours qualifies alone.
Is hosting and maintenance covered?
No. The guidelines exclude them, along with subscriptions, creation of visuals, and advertising.
How long does this take?
You have 6 months after receiving the acknowledgment to submit the complete application, then 3 years to complete the project. The aid arrives at the end, once invoices are verified.
Can we discuss your project together?

Do you have a business or workshop in one of the eligible municipalities and an idea for a website, online ordering, or tool? Write to me or call me before signing anything. We’ll review what qualifies for the Pass, and I’ll provide a clear breakdown of the digital portion, including what’s eligible and what’s not. If it’s not worth the effort, I’ll tell you too.

blog/facture-electronique-artisan-ce-qui.title: Electronic Invoicing: What’s Changing for Tradespeople, Even with Private Clients
blog/facture-electronique-artisan-ce-qui.excerpt: From September 2026, you must be able to receive electronic invoices; in 2027, you will need to issue them. What’s changing for a tradesperson and how to prepare for it.
blog/facture-electronique-artisan-ce-qui.metaTitle: Electronic Invoicing for Tradespeople: Key Changes in 2026 and 2027
blog/facture-electronique-artisan-ce-qui.metaDescription: Mandatory receipt from September 2026, issuance required in 2027: how electronic invoicing impacts tradespeople, including interactions with private clients.

content.text: September 1, 2026, passed quietly in many workshops. Yet, since that date, any business subject to VAT must be able to receive electronic invoices. And in one year, on September 1, 2027, it will be the turn of artisans and small businesses to send them.

One question keeps coming up everywhere on this topic, and it’s one of the most searched on Google: “My clients are private individuals—does this concern me?” The short answer: yes, but not in the way you might think. I build quoting and invoicing tools for artisans, so here’s what’s really changing, case by case, without the jargon. I verified this information in September 2026 on official government websites; the details may still evolve, and your accountant remains the best person to confirm your situation.
Electronic invoicing in two phases
As of September 1, 2026
: all businesses must be able to receive electronic invoices. Large companies and mid-sized businesses must also issue them.
As of September 1, 2027
: SMEs, small businesses, and micro-enterprises will also have to issue them.

An electronic invoice isn’t just a PDF sent by email. It’s a structured file in UBL, CII, or Factur-X format (a PDF embedding its data), transmitted through a platform approved by the state. Your platform sends it to your client’s, while also forwarding the necessary data to the tax authorities.
What’s already mandatory: receiving invoices from your suppliers

This is a point many artisans have overlooked. Large suppliers—like a national wholesaler of materials or a major equipment rental company—must already send you their invoices electronically. To receive them, you need an approved platform.
Concretely: choose a platform from the
official list published by the tax authorities

, open an account there, and ensure your business appears in the directory so your suppliers know where to send their invoices. If you haven’t done this yet, it’s the first thing to address—before even thinking about your own invoices.
Your clients are private individuals: what changes, and what doesn’t
Good news: your invoices to private individuals won’t become electronic. After fixing Mrs. Martin’s water heater, you can still hand her a paper invoice or a PDF.

What changes is e-reporting. Starting September 1, 2027, the data from these sales must be reported to the tax authorities: the daily cumulative amounts and the corresponding VAT, not the details of each invoice. Your platform handles this, at a frequency depending on your VAT scheme. But first, your sales must be recorded there—which is where handwritten invoices become problematic.
And if you’re a micro-entrepreneur without VAT? You’re still affected. The VAT exemption changes the wording on your invoices, but not your obligations under the reform.
You also work with professionals

A plumber working in a restaurant, a mason subcontracted by a general contractor, a carpenter fitting out a shop: as soon as an invoice is sent to a French company, it must be electronic starting September 1, 2027.
Four new details will appear on your invoices at the same time:
the SIREN number of your professional client;
their delivery address, if it differs from their billing address;
the nature of the operation: sale of goods, service provision, or both;
if applicable, the option for VAT payment based on debits.
Start now by recording your professional clients' SIREN numbers in your files. It’s tedious work, but it’s exactly the kind of thing that can hold you up when everything needs to go out on time.
You create your quotes and invoices on Excel or Word

That’s where it gets tricky. Starting September 2027, an invoice typed in Word or Excel and then sent as a PDF to a professional client will no longer be compliant. And for private clients, your sales will have to go through your platform anyway.
You have two simple options:
switch to an invoicing software connected to an approved platform, which many software solutions already offer;
invoice directly from your platform’s space, if it allows it.

If your business is straightforward, an off-the-shelf software will do just fine. I say this all the more willingly since my specialty is custom solutions: they only make sense if your quotes or workflows are truly unique. I’ll explain how to decide between
off-the-shelf software or custom development
You have a custom-built tool or bespoke software

Some artisans have tools tailored to their needs: software that calculates quotes based on their rates, tracks projects, and generates invoices. There’s no question of scrapping everything. Most approved platforms offer a connection for this scenario: your tool generates the invoice in the correct format and sends it to them, and the platform handles the rest.

For a bulky Excel spreadsheet with macros, it’s often the right time to upgrade to a proper tool, whether it’s off-the-shelf or custom-built. That’s exactly the kind of project I handle: connecting an existing tool to a platform or building a quote and invoicing tool tailored to your workflow, ready for 2027. To see what that looks like, I’ve described
an electrician’s custom tool
, from the service request to the invoice.
The plan by September 2027
1. If not already done, choose an approved platform to receive your invoices: this has been mandatory since September 2026.
2. Categorize your clients: individuals on one side, professionals on the other.
3. Complete your professional client file: SIREN number, billing address, delivery address.
4. Choose how you will invoice: market software, platform space, or a custom tool connected to the platform.
5. Test it in the spring of 2027 with a few real invoices, so you don’t discover a problem on September 1st.
6. Talk to your accountant: they see all your invoices and will know what suits your case best.
What you risk if you are not ready

As of now, an invoice that should have been electronic but isn’t incurs a €50 fine, up to a maximum of €15,000 per year. Not having a platform to receive invoices exposes you, after a three-month warning, to a €500 fine, then €1,000 per quarter of delay. A first error corrected on its own, or within 30 days of the administration’s request, is not penalized.
The official details are on the
Discover electronic invoicing
page of the tax authority’s website.
Your questions about electronic invoicing
I’m a self-employed individual without VAT, am I affected?

Yes. You must be able to receive electronic invoices since September 2026, and from September 2027, issue your invoices to professionals electronically and transmit the data of your sales to individuals.
Is a PDF invoice sent by email considered an electronic invoice?
No. An electronic invoice contains structured data (UBL, CII, or Factur-X) and goes through an approved platform. Classic PDF remains possible for your individual clients.
Is the platform paid?

It depends: each platform sets its own prices, and some offer free plans for very small businesses. You are not required to choose the same one as your suppliers or clients: platforms communicate with each other.
All my clients are individuals; can I wait until 2027?
