content.text: "I’d need a website, right?" That’s the phrase I hear most when a tradesman or a small business owner gets in touch with me. And often, after digging a little, I realize that’s not really what they need—or not yet.
what

A showcase website and a business tool are two different things, solving two different problems. Confusing them is the best way to waste money in the wrong place—a pretty website while the real leak is somewhere else. I don’t push either by default: I first look at what’s costing you time or customers, and we go from there.
The Showcase Website: Your Presence, Not Your Workshop

A showcase website is your digital business card. It serves one clear purpose: to help people who are looking for you find you, understand what you do, and get in touch. Showcase your work with photos, your service area, a clear phone number, and a visible contact form.
That’s the right choice if your issue is
visibility

: you’re not showing up on Google, you rely 100% on word-of-mouth, or your Facebook page pales next to the competitor down the street. A well-optimized local website can bring in quote requests while you’re out on a job—without you lifting a finger.
What a showcase website
doesn’t do
: it won’t draft your quotes, track your projects, or chase unpaid invoices. It’s a window display—not a workshop.
The Business Tool (or App): What Saves You Your Evenings
A business tool is the opposite: no one sees it but you and your team. It’s designed to
keep your business running smoothly
day-to-day. In practice, depending on the trade, it might look like this:
generating a clean quote in five minutes, straight from your phone, with your rates already included;
getting an instant overview of where each job stands and who’s handling what this week;
finding a meter photo or a blueprint without digging through three different inboxes;
turning an accepted quote into an invoice without re-entering everything.
This is the right choice if your problem is
organization

: the infamous file `devis_v2_final_vraiment.xlsx`, the Post-it notes on the dashboard of the van, the quote forgotten on a Sunday evening at the kitchen table. There, a website won’t change anything. What you need is a tool tailored to
your
way of working—not a generic software where 80% of the buttons are useless to you and the rest doesn’t quite do what you want.
The real question: where exactly is it breaking down today?
Before choosing, ask yourself a simple question, without beating around the bush:
over the past six months, what has cost you the most—clients who couldn’t find you, or evenings spent dealing with paperwork?
If it’s « they can’t find me » →
a business website
first.
If it’s « I’m drowning in admin » →
a specialized tool
first.
If it’s both… that’s normal, and we’ll tackle that right after.
This question might seem basic, but it avoids the most common mistake: investing in a pretty website while the real money drain is the two hours lost every night on Excel—or doing the opposite.
A concrete example

Take a plumber who’s doing well: two employees, fully booked. He tells me, « I need a website. » We look together. He already has enough clients—he even turns down jobs. His real issue is elsewhere: he writes quotes by hand in the evenings and loses them. Some go out three days late; by the time he sends them, the client has already called a competitor.

A website wouldn’t have helped him. What we did instead: a small tool to generate clean quotes from his phone between jobs, with his prices already saved. Now his quotes go out the same day. For him, that was worth ten business websites.

Conversely, a landscaper just starting out will first need to be found. At this stage, the same tool would be an unnecessary luxury—what he needs are a local site and a few great photos of his projects to land his first clients.
Even in the same sector—or nearly so—needs are opposite. Hence the interest in looking at
your
situation, not the average.
How much does it cost, without beating around the bush?

The fear when talking about « custom-made » is a sky-high quote. It’s not a foregone conclusion. A well-made business website remains a reasonable and controlled budget. And for a specialized tool, you don’t have to build everything at once: start with
a
specific problem—the quotes, the schedule, the follow-up—for a controlled cost, and only expand if it proves its worth.
To give you a benchmark: a tool that solves one of these problems usually costs
between €5,000 and €15,000
at a fixed price, then
€100 to €300 per month
for maintenance. The amount is set in the quote before we start, and everything is explained on my
custom business software in Rennes
page.
The right way to think about it isn’t « how much does it cost » in absolute terms, but « how much does it save or earn me. » Two hours every evening, or three lost quotes per month, add up quickly.
And often, both—but in the right order.

Many businesses need both in the long run. The good news is that you don’t have to do everything at once. Start with the most painful point, fix it, measure the results—and add the rest when it makes sense, and when the first step has paid for itself.
A business website can also become the gateway to a tool: online appointment booking, customer portal, order tracking. But that’s the next step. First, patch the biggest leak.
In short
Business website
= being found and building trust. Issue of
visibility
Specialized tool
= saving time and stopping internal money loss. Issue of
organization
We start with
what costs the most today
, not what shines the brightest.
Some questions I’m often asked
Is a website enough to get more clients?
It helps you get found, provided it’s well-optimized locally and inspires trust. A website that’s invisible on Google won’t bring anyone in.
A custom tool—isn’t that too expensive for a small business?
Not necessarily. You can start by tackling one specific problem within a set budget. The goal isn’t to overhaul everything but to fix the issue costing you the most.
I honestly have no idea which option suits me best.
That’s exactly why we’ll discuss it for ten minutes. By looking at your organization closely, we’ll quickly spot where the leaks are.
Let’s talk?
If you’re unsure, the easiest thing is to chat. I’ll review your organization, tell you honestly where the first bottlenecks are, with a realistic budget estimate—and
if a simple website or an existing tool will do, I’ll let you know
instead of selling you unnecessary custom solutions. You’ll leave with a clear plan, whether you work with me or not.

content.text: I don’t fix cars and I’d be completely unable to change a clutch. But I’ve spent time in garages, watching mechanics juggle a car on the lift, a customer at the counter, and the phone ringing for the third time. And every time, there’s the same object near the cash register: a crammed appointment book full of scribbles, and a phone covered in grease stains.

If you run a garage, alone or with two or three mechanics, you know what I’m talking about. You’re a great technician—but your day is just as much about what happens under the hood as it is about the organization around it.
A garage’s appointment book is a tightrope act.

A customer calls for a service. You check the book, slot them in for Thursday. Then someone else shows up for a breakdown—a car that won’t start. Then the Thursday customer calls back to reschedule. And at some point, you’re not entirely sure who’s coming when, or if you’ll have time for everything.

Paper appointment books work—until you’re under a car, hands deep in the engine, and the phone rings for a booking. You can’t answer, or you scribble it on a scrap of paper that’ll get lost. Result: overlapping slots, waiting customers, and you finishing at 7:30 PM because the day got away from you.

A tool designed for a garage doesn’t perform miracles. But it puts all your appointments in one place, visible at a glance, with estimated times per job. You can instantly see if your day is booked solid or if there’s room. And the customer can even book online while you’re under the car.
The repair quote: the one you ‘do when you have time’

That’s often where the money slips away. A customer leaves their car, you diagnose it, and you need to price it: parts, labor, time. But the quote gets done between repairs, or late at night, from memory.

And while you’re doing that, the customer is waiting. If they wait too long, they’ll call another garage. Or they’ll verbally agree, you’ll do the repair, and when it comes to billing, you realize you underquoted—missed a part, didn’t count an hour of labor. That hour? You’ll never charge it back.

Ask yourself: over the last month, how many hours did you actually spend under the cars, and how many did you bill for? If the gap is fuzzy, it’s probably hundreds of euros lost—not because you’re doing a bad job, but because nothing cleanly connects ‘what you did’ to ‘what you billed.’

A tailored tool lets you pull up a clear quote in minutes, based on your labor rates and standard parts. The customer gets it fast, approves it, and the repair turns into an invoice in one smooth step—nothing forgotten.
Vehicle history: ‘What did you do last time?’
A customer comes back six months later. ‘What did you replace, exactly?’ And then you’re digging through old files or trying to remember. Sometimes you find it. Often, you don’t.

Yet that history is gold: it saves time on diagnostics, reassures the customer, and lets you remind them their timing belt needs changing soon. A garage that tracks its vehicles keeps its customers—and brings them back.

A tool built for you keeps, for every vehicle, what you did, when, and with which parts. Next time the car comes back, everything’s there. You’re no longer dependent on your memory or an overflowing filing cabinet.
Why ‘all-in-one’ garage software ends up ignored

You’ve probably been pitched some massive garage management software. Maybe you’ve got one tucked away somewhere that you never open. Because it does too much, takes ten minutes to log a simple oil change, and wasn’t built for how you actually work.
A tool that slows you down, you won’t use—you’ll go back to the notebook. It’s that simple. The real difference between generic software and a
custom tool
is that the latter fits your garage: your services, your pricing, how you book appointments, your regular customers. Nothing more. Nothing less.
A concrete example
Let’s take Karim, a three-person garage. Before, it was notebooks, spreadsheets, and memory. Appointments overlapped, and he wasted hours redoing quotes.

Today, his appointments are all on one screen, visible to the entire team. A quote is done in five minutes from the workshop. And when a car comes back, he opens its file: the full history is there. Once a week, he checks one thing—the repairs done but not yet invoiced. The list is short, and it no longer contains any omissions.
Karim didn’t become a manager. He simply stopped running after his organization.
A tailored tool for a garage, in concrete terms
Not a bloated system. A tool that does well the few things that matter:
A clear appointment book
, visible to the team, with online booking if you wish.
A repair quote in minutes
, based on your rates and parts.
The vehicle file
with the customer’s full maintenance history.
See at a glance what hasn’t been invoiced yet.
The rest—parts inventory, reminders, accounting—we only add if you truly need it. We start from your daily reality.
In short
The paper appointment book eventually overflows: slots overlap, and the day runs over.
The quotes done "when you have the time" and unbilled hours—that’s where the money slips away.
Vehicle history tracking saves time and builds loyalty—provided you can find it again.
A generic, overly complex software will end up ignored; a tool tailored to your garage, you’ll actually use.

Isn’t this just for big dealerships?

No, it’s actually the opposite. A dealership has staff for management. A neighborhood garage, however, has no one—it’s exactly the kind of place where saving two hours a week makes all the difference.

If you actually use it and it works for you, don’t change anything. If you paid for it but it’s gathering dust because it’s too cumbersome, the issue isn’t finding another one like it—it’s getting a tool you’ll open.
How much does it cost?
It depends on what you need, and sometimes an existing tool is enough—I’ll let you know if that’s the case. The goal is to save you time and stop missed billing, not to sell you software.

We start small: tackle the biggest pain point first (often appointments or quotes), get it up and running quickly, then add the rest gradually.
